m: To exist in large numbers or amounts.
t: Same as « abonder »: waves (unda) overflowing.

m: Pleasant because of shared qualities or interests.
t: Not « congénital ». Congenial = « sympathique »: a congenial colleague is easy company.

m: Hasty and not thorough.
t: Same root as « cursus » and « courir »: you run through it without stopping.

m: Seeming difficult to deal with; intimidating.
t: Danter = dompter: a task so big it tames you. A daunting pile of work.

m: To treat as a god; to worship.
t: Same as « déifier »: make (fier) into a deus.

m: Possible and practical to do.
t: Feasible = « faisable ». A feasibility study is an étude de faisabilité.

m: Disliking other people and avoiding society.
t: Molière’s « Le Misanthrope »: a man who hates mankind.

m: A wrong or inaccurate name or term.
t: Mis + nom: a wrong name. « Un abus de langage ».

m: Failing to take proper care.
t: Same as « négligent ».

m: Belonging to a period other than the one in which it exists.
t: Against time: a smartphone in a Molière play is an « anachronisme ».

m: To desire what belongs to someone else.
t: Same as « convoiter ».

m: Neatly skilful and quick in movement.
e: Middle English defte, variant of daft (gentle, fitting). Germanic.
t: Think « déft »: dexterous fingers. A deft pickpocket, a deft negotiator.

m: Unwilling or unable to believe something.
t: Same as « incrédule ».

m: Harsh-sounding; a mix of loud, unpleasant sounds.
t: Kakos (caca!) + phone: bad sound. The cacophony of a Paris traffic jam.

m: To declare a person officially a saint; to regard as great.
t: Same as « canoniser »: added to the list of saints.

m: Evoking interest or admiration in a powerfully irresistible way; convincing.
t: A compelling argument drives you to agree (compel = contraindre).

m: To struggle to overcome; to assert.
t: Two meanings: compete (contender) and claim. « Il soutient que… » = he contends that…

m: To divide into two sharply contrasting groups.
t: Same as « polariser »: a polarizing debate splits into two poles.

m: To protect and care for lovingly; to hold dear.
t: Same as « chérir »: mon cher.

m: Designed to start fires; tending to stir up conflict.
t: Same as « incendiaire »: an incendiary remark sets the room on fire.

m: To give strength or energy to.
t: In + vigueur: put vigour into someone. An invigorating morning run.

m: No longer produced or used; out of date.
t: Same as « obsolète ».

m: Serving as a typical example or model.
t: From « paradigme »: the perfect pattern. A paradigmatic case.

m: Relating to strongly critical or controversial argument.
t: Same as « polémique »: a war of words.

m: Great depth of insight or knowledge.
t: Profondeur: a deep thought, with a deep bottom (fundus).

m: Accurately predicting what will happen.
t: Same as « prophétique ».

m: Free from disturbance; calm.
t: Same as « tranquille ».

m: Not friendly; distant and cool.
e: From Dutch sailing term a + luff: keeping the ship to windward, away from the lee shore.
t: Keeping your boat away from everyone else. An aloof manager stays apart.

m: A continuous loud banging or ringing noise.
e: Latin clangor (sound of a trumpet), imitative of the sound.
t: Hear the clang of metal: « clangor » is a loud ringing din. Cousin of « clameur ».

m: Based on what is generally done; traditional.
t: Same as « conventionnel »: following the usual agreement.

m: Able to be seen or noticed.
t: Same root as « discerner »: you can tell it apart.

m: Mysterious and difficult to understand.
t: Same as « énigmatique »: the Mona Lisa’s smile.

m: No longer close or affectionate; alienated.
t: Made « étranger » to someone: an estranged husband is a stranger now.

m: Lacking restraint in spending or in behaviour.
t: Same as « extravagant »: wandering outside the limits.

m: Overly imaginative and unrealistic.
t: Fancy = fantaisie. A fanciful plan lives only in the imagination.

m: Tending to intrude; spreading harmfully.
t: Same as « invasif »: invasive species, invasive surgery.

m: Not strict or careful enough.
t: Same as « laxiste »: loose rules, lax security.

m: To treat as insignificant or peripheral.
t: Same as « marginaliser »: push to the margin of the page.

m: Intended to correct or improve something deficient.
t: A remedy: remedial classes are « cours de rattrapage ».

m: To describe or regard as worthy of disgrace.
e: Greek stigma (mark, brand burned on the skin).
t: Same as « stigmatiser »: to brand someone.

m: Completely and absolutely.
e: From utter (outer, extreme), Old English ūtera, from ūt (out). Germanic.
t: To the outermost limit: utterly ridiculous = tout à fait ridicule.

m: Tired; also, cautious about something because of past experience.
t: Not « wary » (prudent). Weary = las: weary of the job market.

m: Excessively or aggressively patriotic; prejudiced in favour of one's own group.
e: French chauvin, from Nicolas Chauvin, a legendary Napoleonic soldier of fanatical loyalty.
t: A French word! Chauvin, the fanatical soldier of Napoleon. Same as « chauvin ».

m: Persistent and determined.
e: From dog: with the stubborn grip of a dog. Germanic.
t: Dogged like a dog on a bone: dogged determination = « une ténacité de bouledogue ».

m: Believing oneself inherently deserving of privileges; having a right to.
f: qui se croit tout permis; ayant droit
t: Two senses: having a right (entitled to a refund) or arrogant (an entitled brat).

m: Holding firmly to an opinion or course of action; stubborn.
t: Per + tenace: very tenacious. Not « pertinent ».

m: Based on personal feelings rather than facts.
t: Same as « subjectif »: opinion, not fact.

m: To undermine the power of an established system.
t: Same as « subversif »: turn it upside down from below.

m: Willing to do dishonest things for money; corrupt.
t: Same as « vénal »: someone whose loyalty is for sale.

m: Making a loud and confused noise.
t: A clamour (clameur): a clamorous crowd shouts together.

m: Able to be explained.
t: Same as « explicable ». Opposite: inexplicable.

m: Showing a lack of respect for people or things usually taken seriously.
t: Same as « irrévérencieux »: no révérence.

m: To feel intense dislike or disgust for.
e: Old English lāthian (to be hateful), from lāth (hostile). Germanic.
t: Loathe, hate. Not to be confused with « loath » (reluctant, no e).

m: To speak harmful untruths about; (adj.) evil in nature.
t: Same as « malin » (as in tumeur maligne): malign = speak ill of.

m: Serious and strict, especially in manner.
t: A stern teacher is strict. (Also the back of a ship: another meaning.)

m: To make more noticeable; to emphasize.
t: Same as « accentuer ».

m: Based on guesswork rather than proof.
t: Same as « conjecture » (une conjecture): a guess.

m: In a state of moral or cultural decline; luxuriously self-indulgent.
t: Same as « décadent »: Rome in decline. A decadent chocolate cake.

m: Tending to attract attention because of exuberance or confidence.
t: Straight from French: flaming. Le style gothique flamboyant.

m: Done at random or without careful judgement.
t: Not « discrimé »: no distinguishing. Indiscriminate bombing hits everything.

m: Lasting for a very short time.
t: Same as « momentané ».

m: To make legally void; to cancel out the effect of.
t: Make nul: « rendre nul et non avenu ».

m: Present everywhere at the same time.
t: Same as « omniprésent ».

m: To drive out or expel from a position.
e: Anglo-French ouster, Old French oster (to remove), Latin obstare (to stand in the way).
t: French « ôter »: to remove. A CEO ousted by the board.

m: So intense it seems almost touchable; easily perceived.
t: Same as « palpable »: you could touch it. Palpable tension.

m: Underhand or unscrupulous behaviour.
t: A skull and dagger! Shady skullduggery in the boardroom = « des magouilles ».

m: Of little value or importance.
t: French « trivial » means vulgar. English trivial = unimportant: « sans importance ».

m: Offering nothing that is stimulating or challenging; dull.
e: Latin vapidus (flat, flavourless, like wine that has lost its spirit).
t: Flat like a wine gone off: « fade ». A vapid conversation.

m: Courteous and considerate behaviour; mutual respect between states.
t: From « comité »? No: comity = friendly civility. « Comity of nations »: states respecting each other’s laws.
